The person is building or affiliated with an aesthetic networking community and works in a content creation or consulting capacity within the medical aesthetics space. They were researching CME (Continuing Medical Education) accreditation pathways on behalf of a physician named Neda, who owns a med spa and training institute and is a licensed provider and doctor. The person wanted to understand the best routes for Neda to get her institute CME-accredited so that students can earn credits through her programs.

Claude explained two personal credentialing options for Neda as a physician instructor — AAAM board certification and IAPAM training — and outlined two accreditation paths for the institute itself: Joint Providership (partnering with an existing ACCME-accredited organization like Global Education Group) versus pursuing full ACCME accreditation directly, which takes six to ten months. Claude recommended starting with Joint Providership and transitioning to full accreditation after one to two years of documented CME activity.

The person then asked Claude to draft a follow-up email to Neda. The email covered four areas: expressing enthusiasm about a recent filming visit to Neda's med spa and institute, expressing interest in future collaboration, committing to send video edits for her social media use once available, and proposing to host an aesthetic networking group in Neda's classroom. The CME accreditation advice was incorporated into the email, framed as a tip passed along from a colleague to keep the tone personal rather than prescriptive.

Good context. There are actually two separate goals here, and she needs to think about both. Here's the full picture:

**Goal 1: Her personal CME credentials as a physician instructor**

As a physician/provider launching a training institute, she first needs strong personal credentials to teach with authority. Best options:

- **AAAM (American Academy of Aesthetic Medicine)** - offers board certification courses with CME credits, reviewed and approved at the highest levels of accreditation, jointly provided with Medical Academy LLC. This is the most respected physician-level credential for aesthetics instructors globally.
- **IAPAM** - has helped over 15,000 physicians expand their skills since 2006, with hands-on Botox and aesthetic medicine training from board-certified dermatologists in Scottsdale, AZ, including CME credits. Good if she wants clinical depth plus a business framework.
- **AmSpa Medical Spa Show** - delivers CME content and is the largest industry conference. Good for visibility and networking with other KOLs, not just credentials.

**Goal 2: Making her institute itself CME-accredited (so students earn credits)**

This is the bigger, more complex piece. There are two paths:

**Path A: Joint Providership (faster, lower barrier)**
Partner with an already-accredited organization to co-deliver your courses under their accreditation umbrella. Companies like Global Education Group are ACCME-accredited and provide joint providership, allowing other organizations to offer AMA PRA Category 1 Credits through the partnership. This is how most new aesthetics institutes start. Much faster than going direct.

**Path B: Full ACCME Accreditation (longer, more prestigious)**
Accredit the institute itself directly with ACCME. The process: start with a Confirmation of Intent form and initial accreditation fee, then submit a written self-study report and evidence of performance-in-practice before an accreditation interview with trained volunteer surveyors. The full process takes 6 to 10 months depending on readiness. If most of her learners are in-state or contiguous states, she may actually go through the state medical society instead of ACCME directly.

**My recommendation for her:**

Start with Joint Providership through an existing accreditor while she builds her institute's track record, then pursue full ACCME accreditation after 1 to 2 years of documented CME activity. On the personal credential side, AAAM board certification is the most globally recognized for a physician building an institute with training authority.

MDs/DOs/PAs: This activity has been planned and implemented in accordance with the accreditation requirements and policies of the Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME) through the joint providership of Oakstone Publishing and The American Association of Aesthetic Medicine & Surgery (AAAMS). Oakstone Publishing is accredited by the ACCME to provide continuing medical education for physicians. RNs/NPs: This activity has been planned and implemented in accordance with the accreditation requirements and policies of the American Nurses Credentialing Center’s Commission on Accreditation through the joint providership of Oakstone Publishing and The American Association of Aesthetic Medicine & Surgery (AAAMS). Oakstone Publishing is accredited as a provider of nursing continuing professional development by the American Nurses Credentialing Center’s Commission on Accreditation.

Describe the 4Rs of aesthetics. Explain the concept of Facial Beautification.

Good context. There are actually two separate goals here, and she needs to think about both. Here's the full picture:

**Goal 1: Her personal CME credentials as a physician instructor**

As a physician/provider launching a training institute, she first needs strong personal credentials to teach with authority. Best options:

- **AAAM (American Academy of Aesthetic Medicine)** - offers board certification courses with CME credits, reviewed and approved at the highest levels of accreditation, jointly provided with Medical Academy LLC. This is the most respected physician-level credential for aesthetics instructors globally.
- **IAPAM** - has helped over 15,000 physicians expand their skills since 2006, with hands-on Botox and aesthetic medicine training from board-certified dermatologists in Scottsdale, AZ, including CME credits. Good if she wants clinical depth plus a business framework.
- **AmSpa Medical Spa Show** - delivers CME content and is the largest industry conference. Good for visibility and networking with other KOLs, not just credentials.

**Goal 2: Making her institute itself CME-accredited (so students earn credits)**

This is the bigger, more complex piece. There are two paths:

**Path A: Joint Providership (faster, lower barrier)**
Partner with an already-accredited organization to co-deliver your courses under their accreditation umbrella. Companies like Global Education Group are ACCME-accredited and provide joint providership, allowing other organizations to offer AMA PRA Category 1 Credits through the partnership. This is how most new aesthetics institutes start. Much faster than going direct.

**Path B: Full ACCME Accreditation (longer, more prestigious)**
Accredit the institute itself directly with ACCME. The process: start with a Confirmation of Intent form and initial accreditation fee, then submit a written self-study report and evidence of performance-in-practice before an accreditation interview with trained volunteer surveyors. The full process takes 6 to 10 months depending on readiness. If most of her learners are in-state or contiguous states, she may actually go through the state medical society instead of ACCME directly.

**My recommendation for her:**

Start with Joint Providership through an existing accreditor while she builds her institute's track record, then pursue full ACCME accreditation after 1 to 2 years of documented CME activity. On the personal credential side, AAAM board certification is the most globally recognized for a physician building an institute with training authority.

Want me to identify specific joint providership partners she could approach, or map out the ACCME application timeline in detail?

variants.body:
Neda,

I just have to say, what an incredible time I had filming at your med spa and institute. The space, the energy, the way you've built everything — it was genuinely inspiring to be there, and I left feeling so fired up about what you're creating.

I'm so excited to see what's possible between us as we move forward. I think there's a really natural fit for collaboration, and I'd love to explore what that looks like together.

As soon as I get the edits back, I'll send everything over so you have it ready to use for your socials. I want to make sure you have content that does your space justice.

On another note, I've been working on getting an aesthetic networking group up and running here in the area, and honestly, after seeing your classroom setup, I would absolutely love to entertain the idea of hosting one there. It's such a perfect space for it, and I think the community we'd bring together would love it.

Also, I mentioned your situation to a colleague of mine who's been through the process of getting her institute CME accredited, and she shared some really helpful insight I wanted to pass along. She said the smartest starting point for a physician building a training institute is pursuing Joint Providership first. Basically, you partner with an already ACCME-accredited organization to co-deliver your courses under their accreditation umbrella, so your students can earn AMA PRA Category 1 Credits right away without waiting 6 to 10 months for full accreditation. Companies like Global Education Group do exactly this. Once you've built a track record of documented CME activity, usually after a year or two, you apply for full ACCME accreditation directly. The full process involves a self-study report, evidence of performance, and an accreditation interview, and typically takes 6 to 10 months. On the personal credential side, she highly recommended AAAM board certification as the most respected physician-level credential for someone in your position, especially if you want to teach and train with real authority. It's globally recognized and a strong foundation for everything you're building.

Hope this is helpful as you're mapping things out. I'm rooting for you and would love to be part of the journey in whatever way makes sense.

Talk soon,
Bethany
